questions.stem: A healthy pregnant client with an uncomplicated pregnancy asks about exercise. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Limit activity to gentle stretching because moderate aerobic exercise is discouraged even when pregnancy is uncomplicated and no contraindication is present.","B":"Aim for about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week when there are no obstetric or medical contraindications, adjusting activity as needed.","C":"Maintain the pre-pregnancy intensity target without adjusting for symptoms or obstetric changes because exercise recommendations remain fixed throughout pregnancy.","D":"Begin vigorous conditioning even if previously sedentary because pregnancy is an appropriate time to increase exercise intensity rapidly for cardiovascular benefit."}}
questions.rationale: For a healthy person with an uncomplicated pregnancy and no contraindications, regular physical activity is safe and desirable. Option B is correct because ACOG recommends about 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, with adjustment as needed. Option A is unnecessarily restrictive. Option C ignores symptoms and obstetric changes. Option D inappropriately recommends rapid progression to vigorous conditioning for someone who may have been sedentary.
questions.source_name: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Exercise During Pregnancy
questions.source_detail: Current ACOG guidance states that physical activity is safe and desirable in uncomplicated pregnancy without contraindications and recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week.

questions.stem: A client frequently misses doses because the medication schedule is complex and easy to forget. Which intervention best supports adherence?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Increase the number of daily dosing times when possible because a more complex schedule makes each dose more noticeable and therefore improves adherence.","B":"Focus on medication education without asking about cost, side effects, or confusion because those barriers are separate from adherence counseling.","C":"Simplify the regimen when possible, link doses to daily routines, and use pill organizers or electronic reminders tailored to the client's barriers.","D":"Use counseling without reminder tools because pill organizers, routines, and electronic prompts add complexity without improving day-to-day adherence."}}
questions.rationale: Adherence improves when regimens and reminders are made easier and barriers are addressed. Option C is correct because AHRQ recommends simplifying dosing when possible, linking doses to routines, and using pill organizers or electronic reminders. Option A increases complexity. Option B ignores common adherence barriers. Option D rejects practical reminder strategies that AHRQ recommends.
questions.source_name: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality — Help Patients Take Medicine Correctly: Tool 16
questions.source_detail: AHRQ Tool 16, last reviewed April 2024 and current on the AHRQ site, recommends simplifying medication schedules when possible, addressing barriers, linking doses to daily routines, and using pill organizers or electronic reminders.

questions.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of anorexia nervosa?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recurrent episodes of eating unusually large amounts with loss of control and distress, without compensatory behavior or a persistently low body weight.","B":"Markedly restricted intake, intense fear of gaining weight, low body weight, distorted body image, and denial of the seriousness of low weight.","C":"Recurrent binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting or laxative use while body weight may remain in an expected or higher range.","D":"Restricted intake driven by food texture, sensory features, or fear of choking without a primary fear of weight gain or distorted body image."}}
questions.rationale: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by severe restriction, intense fear of weight gain, low body weight, distorted body image, and often denial of the seriousness of low weight. Option B is correct. Option A better resembles binge-eating disorder. Option C describes a binge-purge pattern consistent with bulimia nervosa. Option D better resembles ARFID, where restriction is not primarily driven by weight-gain fear or distorted body image.
questions.source_name: National Institute of Mental Health — Eating Disorders: What You Need to Know
questions.source_detail: Current NIMH guidance lists extreme restriction, intense fear of weight gain, extreme thinness/low weight, distorted body image, and denial of the seriousness of low weight among characteristic features of anorexia nervosa.

questions.stem: A child with autism spectrum disorder becomes distressed by unexpected procedures. The child needs a blood draw that was not part of the usual routine. Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Give a simple advance explanation and use a visual schedule or social story to show what will happen, preserving predictability before care begins today.","B":"Give a detailed verbal explanation after the procedure begins because advance preparation may increase distress when the child's routine is changing.","C":"Use figurative language and indirect hints before the procedure because abstract communication promotes flexibility more effectively than concrete information.","D":"Change the care routine frequently without advance explanation because repeated unexpected changes are the preferred way to reduce distress over time."}}
questions.rationale: Predictability and concrete preparation can reduce distress for many children with autism. Option A is correct because CDC describes consistency, visual supports, and Social Stories that give simple descriptions of what to expect. Option B delays preparation until after the procedure begins. Option C relies on abstract figurative language rather than concrete information. Option D deliberately increases unexpected change rather than predictability.
questions.source_name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Treatment and Intervention for Autism Spectrum Disorder
questions.source_detail: CDC guidance rechecked August 14, 2026 notes that people with autism may thrive on consistency and visual learning; routines can be written or drawn, verbal instructions can be paired with visual supports, and Social Stories can explain what to expect.

questions.stem: Which pattern best supports further evaluation for ADHD rather than a brief or single-setting attention problem?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Inattention has persisted for 8 months at school, but similar symptoms are not reported at home, with relatives, or during other activities.","B":"Inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity has persisted for at least 6 months, occurs in two or more settings, and impairs daily functioning.","C":"Symptoms occur at home and school and interfere with functioning, but they have been present for about 6 weeks following a major family disruption.","D":"Similar behaviors are reported at home and school for more than 6 months, but functioning and development remain age-appropriate despite the behaviors."}}
questions.rationale: ADHD diagnosis requires a persistent developmentally inappropriate pattern that causes impairment and occurs in more than one setting. Option B is correct because it includes at least 6 months of symptoms, two or more settings, and functional impairment. Option A is limited to one setting. Option C has lasted only about 6 weeks and follows a major disruption that may better explain the behavior. Option D lacks impairment despite persistent behaviors.
questions.source_name: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Care of ADHD in Children
questions.source_detail: CDC clinical guidance updated June 1, 2026 states ADHD symptoms must persist at least 6 months, occur in two or more settings, and interfere with or reduce the quality of functioning.
